sentences.text: Through this part, higher capital gains lower a typical person's the predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less slowly at first, then faster, falling faster once the gain rises above about 3912 US dollars: from about 55% at 0 to about 9% at 6849 US dollars, flattening out near the bottom because the predicted chance cannot go much lower; but for people not living in a family the curve bends once instead.
For people not living in a family, gains add nothing until about 3756 US dollars, then lower the chance steadily, from about 69% to about 10%, against about 55% to about 9% for everyone else.
Through it, not living in a family lowers the chance from about 55% to about 39%.

This part adds up most characteristics, each on its own: a higher education level lowers a typical person's the predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less steadily, from about 78% at 7 to about 31% at 13 on the 1-16 scale, as do higher capital losses (about 55% at 0 to about 27% at 1887 US dollars) and longer working hours (about 65% at 24 to about 46% at 55 hours a week).

A marital status other than married (to a civilian or to a member of the armed forces) or widowed raises it to about 83% and a relationship in the household other than husband or wife to about 82%, while being a wife lowers it to about 29%; being a woman raises it to about 72%.

Compared with a professional job, farming or fishing raises it to about 83%, other service work to about 81% and a missing occupation to about 78%, while an executive or managerial job lowers it to about 48%; working without pay raises it to above 99% (the model has little data on this, n = 17).

Being born in Colombia raises it to about 99%, in Trinidad and Tobago to about 94% and in Laos to about 83% (the model has little data on this, n = 17), while being born in Portugal lowers it to about 28% and in Yugoslavia to about 32%; a highest education of 5th-6th grade lowers it to about 33%.

This part adds up nine single-category adjustments: being born in Scotland raises a typical person's the predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less to above 99% (the model has little data on this, n = 16), and handling or cleaning raises it to about 73%.

Working for the federal government lowers it to about 42%, being another relative or unmarried to about 47% and being Asian or Pacific Islander to about 51%, while being born outside the United States raises it to about 63%.
Handling or cleaning raises it more for people who are not Asian or Pacific Islander: from about 55% to about 79%, against about 57% to about 72%.

Through this part, older age lowers a typical person's the predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less steadily up to about 38 years, then no further: from about 84% at 22 to about 50% at 58 years.

lead.text: For a typical person (a 37-year-old White married man born in the United States, a high-school graduate in a professional job in the private sector, working 40 hours a week, with no capital gains or losses) the model predicts a chance of an income of $50,000 or less of about 55%; it adds up four parts: capital gains, most characteristics added up on their own, a set of single-category adjustments, and youth.

evidence.text: Through it, a typical person's chance goes from about 55% at 0 to about 9% at 6849 US dollars, slowly at first, then faster once the gain rises above about 3912 US dollars, flattening out near the bottom because the predicted chance cannot go much lower; but for people not living in a family the curve bends once instead.
For people not living in a family, gains add nothing until about 3756 US dollars, then lower the chance steadily, from about 69% to about 10%, against about 55% to about 9% for everyone else.
Not living in a family lowers a typical person's chance through it from about 55% to about 39%.

reference_patient.definition: the typical patient: the median training patient for every number and the most common training category for every category (not a real patient)

confidence_rules.clearly: a meaningful change in predicted risk for a typical patient (at least 5% points), the test split agrees (same sign, and its bootstrap interval over test patients excludes no benefit), and every group has at least 20 training patients

confidence_rules.on the training data only: the test split disagrees (opposite sign, or no benefit on test patients) or is unclear (its interval includes no benefit), or no test check is available
confidence_rules.slightly: the change in predicted risk for a typical patient is below 5% points
confidence_rules.the model has little data on this: a compared group has fewer than 20 training patients

summary.text: The model treats a higher education level as clearly lowering the predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less steadily: for a typical person, it goes from about 78% at 7 on the 1-16 scale to about 31% at 13 on the 1-16 scale.

The model treats a higher capital gains as clearly lowering the predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less slowly at first, then faster for most people, but for people not living in a family it has a threshold: for a typical person, it goes from about 55% at 0 US dollars to about 9% at 6849 US dollars, flattening out near the bottom because the predicted risk cannot go much lower.

For a typical person, the model gives a higher predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less if the country of birth is Colombia (about 99%) than if the country of birth is the United States (about 55%) (on the training data only).

Through one part of the model, capital gains only clearly lowers the predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less once it rises above about 3912 US dollars: for a typical such person, going from 0 US dollars to 5013 US dollars moves it from about 55% to about 40%; this holds for most people, but for people not living in a family it differs.

The model gives a clearly higher predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less if the occupation is handlers or cleaners than if occupation is something other than handlers or cleaners, and even more so if race is something other than Asian or Pacific Islander: for a typical person, going from occupation other than handlers or cleaners to handlers or cleaners moves the predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less from about 55% to about 79% if race is something other than Asian or Pacific Islander, and from about 57% to about 72% if the recorded race is Asian or Pacific Islander.
